source.authors: Lidia Sukovata, Aleksander Dziuk, Radosław Plewa, Tomasz Jaworski
source.title: The Effect of Trap Color on Catches of Monochamus galloprovincialis and Three Most Numerous Non-Target Insect Species

method: field experiment: lured traps of four colours, catches per trap, GLMM with Dunnett comparison against white
conditions: Wild pine sawyers caught in the field in pure Scots pine stands (Poland; the 2019 experiment in two 83-year-old pine stands of Międzychód Forest District only, the 2020 experiment in Międzychód and Wronki Forest Districts); cross-vane IBL-5 traps hung 4 to 6 m above ground, every trap baited with Galloprotect Pack lures, so the response is to coloured traps on a pheromone-kairomone lure, not to colour alone. Randomized complete block design, one trap of each colour per block, traps about 100 m apart; the text does not say how colours were placed within a block. Analysis: generalised linear mixed model with block as random factor, Wald chi-square for colour, Dunnett comparisons with the unpainted white reference trap, alpha 0.05. Trap colour was set by painting the coroplast vanes (2019: twice with mattish acrylic spray paints, then a PTFE treatment that left the surfaces shiny); the authors did not measure the reflectance of the painted traps and give only theoretical colour values, so brightness and UV reflectance were neither matched nor measured, and painted traps differ from the unpainted white reference in surface as well as colour. Trap counts are a capture outcome, so attraction, landing and retention are not separated, and no detection threshold is measured. 2019 experiment: 14 blocks in two stands, traps set 24 to 25 June and checked 1 and 9 July; colours pastel yellow, cyan blue, reseda green and unpainted white. Estimated marginal means +/- SE: females 40.7 +/- 4.50 per white trap, lowest 28.7 +/- 3.65 in cyan blue; males 4.6 +/- 0.88 (cyan blue) to 6.2 +/- 1.08 (pastel yellow); both sexes 46.8 +/- 4.87 in unpainted white traps, slightly higher than in the other traps. Same paper: in the 2020 experiment colour had a significant effect (see the other record).
quote: We found no significant difference in the catches of M. galloprovincialis of either sex when compared to the white traps.

source.authors: Lidia Sukovata, Aleksander Dziuk, Radosław Plewa, Tomasz Jaworski
source.title: The Effect of Trap Color on Catches of Monochamus galloprovincialis and Three Most Numerous Non-Target Insect Species

method: field experiment: lured traps of six colours, catches per trap, GLMM with Dunnett comparison against white
conditions: Wild pine sawyers caught in the field in pure Scots pine stands (Poland, Międzychód and Wronki Forest Districts); cross-vane IBL-5 traps hung 4 to 6 m above ground, every trap baited with Galloprotect Pack lures, so the response is to coloured traps on a pheromone-kairomone lure, not to colour alone. The 2020 materials and design are said to be similar to 2019 (randomized complete block design, one trap of each colour per block, traps about 100 m apart); in 2020 the 10 blocks were laid out 3 x 2 or 6 x 1 as the terrain dictated, and 2020 spacing and within-block placement are not stated. Analysis: generalised linear mixed model with block as random factor, Wald chi-square for colour, Dunnett comparisons with the unpainted white reference trap, alpha 0.05. Vanes were painted twice with glossy acrylic paints and treated twice with dry PTFE, and the pure white looked rather yellowish on the traps; the authors did not measure the reflectance of the painted traps, so brightness and UV reflectance were neither matched nor measured; painted pure white caught significantly fewer females and males than unpainted white, so painting changed catches apart from hue. Trap counts are a capture outcome, so attraction, landing and retention are not separated, and no detection threshold is measured. 2020 experiment: 10 blocks in the two forest districts, traps set 29 to 30 June and checked 15 and 29 July; deep orange, light blue, pine green, jet black, pure white and unpainted white (chosen as colours with lower theoretical reflectance values than those of 2019, not measured). Colour effect on females chi2 = 36.6, df = 5, p < 0.0001; males chi2 = 15.6, df = 5, p = 0.0079; totals chi2 = 29.5, df = 5, p < 0.0001. In the same series female catches in light blue (5.3 +/- 1.12), pure white (5.6 +/- 1.15) and pine green (6.6 +/- 1.30) traps differed significantly from unpainted white, while jet black (8.9 +/- 1.61) was borderline (p = 0.0528); male catches differed only in pure white (1.5 +/- 0.46) and light blue (1.6 +/- 0.48). The 2019 series with other colours gave no significant difference (see the other record). Laboratory two-plate choice tests in the same paper are not used here.
quote: The unpainted white traps captured the highest numbers of females (14.0 ± 2.32 beetles/trap), males (4.7 ± 1.11 beetles/trap), and beetles of both sexes (18.6 ± 3.08 beetles/trap).
note: Sentence read in two abutting pieces, start and end confirmed; the colour-effect statistics come from the preceding Results sentence (read in three abutting pieces) and the per-colour means from the paper's text, not from the quote. Licence as in the other record (CC BY 4.0 vor on Crossref). Not on main.

source.title: Morphological and olfactory tree traits influence the susceptibility and suitability of the apple species Malus domestica and M. sylvestris to the florivorous weevil Anthonomus pomorum (Coleoptera: Curculionidae)

method: behavioural: still-air dual-choice olfactometer arena, apple twigs with blossom buds versus wire control
conditions: Adults collected from Malus domestica trees by limb-jarring in a botanical garden (post-diapause, mid-March to mid-April 2017), so field-collected from M. domestica, not naive and of unknown sex (sex not recorded). Still-air dual-choice arena (Petri dish with two pipette-tip holes 70 mm apart); stimulus a roughly 5 cm apple twig with 5 +/- 1 blossom buds against a wire model twig as control; 16 C, 70% RH; weevils food-deprived 24 h, acclimatised 90 min, observed 180 min, choice recorded at the end; each weevil used once, new twigs and clean dish per trial. Side randomisation or switching of twig positions is not reported, and the zone counted as a choice is not specified. One-sample chi-square tests. Control versus blank (n = 30) showed no preference (chi2 = 0.14, p = 0.71). Responsiveness 56 to 62% when a blossom-bud twig was offered, 23.3% for control versus blank, so many weevils made no choice. The paper's volatile table has internal inconsistencies, which do not affect these bioassays. n = 50 weevils per comparison.
quote: Weevils that were tested in bioassays for their preference for volatiles from apple blossom buds versus controls, significantly preferred M. sylvestris (χ2 = 6.53; p = 0.01), but not M. domestica over the controls (χ2 = 0.57; p = 0.45).

source.authors: Kim C. Heuel, Tim A. Haßlberger, Manfred Ayasse, Hannah Burger
source.title: Floral Trait Preferences of Three Common wild Bee Species

method: behavioural: two-choice test with yellow versus blue cardboard artificial flowers, first approach per bee
conditions: Free-flying females of a ground-nesting aggregation in the Ulm University Botanical Garden, tested inside a mobile 1.5 m flight cage set above the nesting aggregation (the text does not say outright that the bees came from that aggregation); tests ran 8 am to 1 pm in May and August of 2022 and 2023. Two-choice test with artificial flowers (die-cut 3.3 cm cardboard disks) on green paper: wooden board with three flower pairs, 8 cm apart within a pair and at least 16 cm between pairs, board turned 90 degrees every 10 min, flowers renewed every 20 min; only the first choice of each female approaching the board (within 5 cm) was noted. Experiments were run when about 30 females were active in the cage and repeated three to four times for L. villosulum because of low participation; bees were not marked and some individuals may have taken part more than once, and the total number of bees tested is not given. Binomial GLMs with species as a fixed factor, then per-species models. Yellow cardboard colour angle 146 degrees, blue near maximum opposition in the bee colour hexagon; achromatic contrast against the green background similar but not identical (blue 0.217, yellow 0.234), and the authors offer yellow's slightly higher contrast against the green background as a possible explanation of the B. terrestris yellow preference, a difference that applies equally to this test; in the same paper's achromatic-contrast test L. villosulum showed no overall preference (p = 0.227) but preferred yellow over light-yellow flowers (p = 0.0121), so achromatic contrast may contribute to its yellow choice. The reflectance spectra are only in a supplement. In the same paper Osmia bicornis showed no hue preference (p = 0.339); that species and the commercially reared Bombus terrestris are not logged.
quote: Lasioglossum villosulum (p < 0.001) and B. terrestris (p < 0.001) both strongly preferred yellow over blue flowers.
note: Whole sentence read in one piece, start and end confirmed; the B. terrestris clause is not used for any value. conditions: Free-flying females of a ground-nesting aggregation in the Ulm University Botanical Garden, tested inside a mobile 1.5 m flight cage set above the nesting aggregation (the text does not say outright that the bees came from that aggregation); tests ran 8 am to 1 pm in May and August of 2022 and 2023. Scent: a complex 12-compound mixture against each of three simple 4-compound mixtures, 30 microlitres (30 ng of substance) per flower, mixture as random factor. GC-EAD in the same paper: myrcene in mixture 3 elicited a response in 66% of the six L. villosulum antennae tested; most of the 12 compounds were active in all tested antennae of the wild bee species. source.authors: Orlando J. Luis, João M. Gago
source.title: Perception of Dissolved Food-Related Compounds by the Sea Urchin Paracentrotus lividus (Echinodermata: Echinoidea)

method: behavioural: pairs of 2 x 2 cm cloth simulacra, one soaked in the stimulus and one in seawater, placed together between the spines of the aboral surface of the same urchin; 30 min assays
conditions: Adult wild-collected urchins (test diameter 40 to 50 mm, collected at Cabo Raso, Cascais, Portugal in September), then held in a recirculating seawater system on whole yellow maize, kombu (Laminaria ochroleuca) or both, fed twice weekly for 8 months; a fourth group of wild urchins recollected 15 days before testing and kept unfed. 30 urchins per stimulus in each diet group and in the wild group (figure caption gives N = 150 per diet pooled over five stimuli). Stimuli in this part: glucose 10%, soluble starch 10%, sucrose 10%, olive oil 10% and a 22-amino acid mixture 1 mM. Sex not reported; random assignment of blank and stimulus to position is not described. Captive diet is a confound for the nutritional-state comparison. The first sentence of the same Results passage says that the frequency of feeding responses was independent of the stimulus (P > 0.05, df = 3) but clearly dependent on nutritional state (P < 0.001, df = 3); urchins fed only kombu fronds responded more often than those on any other diet or unfed ones (P < 0.001, df = 1); in many instances the urchins carried neither simulacrum to the mouth; and the sentence ending 'This was the case for the 22-amino acid mixture, olive oil, sucrose, and glucose (P > 0.05)' carries the nulls. In the wider paper 41 stimuli at 1% were tested in batches of eight urchins, with 30 of 41 carried to the mouth more often than blanks and sucrose among those not different from blanks.
where: Results, Contact Food Detection, Long-Term Nutritional State Effects
quote: However, regardless of diet, when soluble starch was the tested stimulus, the sea urchins clearly showed a preference for the respective simulacrum relative to the blank one (P < 0.05).
